div.head: II Atr 4
div.ab: Gyf man beo æt his æhtan bereafod, ⁊ he wite of hwilcum scipe, agyfe steoresman ða æhta oððon gange feowra sum tó ⁊ oðsace — ⁊ beo him sylf fifta —, þæt he hit ariht name, swa hit ær geforword wæs.

Si homo sit de pecunia sua robatus et sciat, in qua naui, reddat steoresman (id est gubernator) pecuniam illam uel cum quatuor iuret — et idem sit quintus —, quod per rectitudinem cepit, sicut antea prelocutum erit.

[Be ðon ðe mon on scipe bereafod sy.] Gyf man beo æt his æhtan bereafod, ⁊ he wite of hwilcum scipe, agyfe steoresman ða æhta oððon gange feowra sum tó ⁊ oðsace—⁊ beo him sylf fifta—þæt he hit ariht name, swa hit ær geforword wæs.

(Darüber, dass jemand an Bord beraubt worden ist. Ld) Wenn jemand an seinen Gütern beraubt worden ist, und er [als Kläger bestimmt] weiss, von (auf Quadr.) welchem Schiffe [dies geschah], so gebe [dessen] Steuermann die Güter heraus oder trete mit vier [Eideshelfern] hin und schwöre sich rein — und er selbst sei Fünfter —, dass er es rechtmässig genommen habe, wie es vorher abgemacht worden sei.

(Of someone robbed on board ship. Ld) If anyone has been robbed of his goods, and he knows [as plaintiff, for certain] from (on, Quadr.) which ship [it happened], let [its] steersman give back the goods or come forward with four [oath-helpers] and clear himself — he himself being the fifth — [swearing] that he took it lawfully, as was previously agreed.

If anyone has been robbed of his goods and he knows the ship by which it has been done, the captain shall restore the goods or shall go with four compurgators—himself making a fifth—and deny [the charge, proving] that he was justified in taking them, according to the terms laid down above.

If a man is robbed of his goods, and he knows by which ship, the steersman is to give back the goods, or to go with four others, being himself the fifth, and deny [the charge, swearing] that he took it lawfully, as it was agreed upon above.

Eines Nordischen Schiffes; gegen Nicolas Hist. Engl. navy I 21. —Von hier ab wird der Rechtsgang im Streit zwischen je einem beider Vertragschliesser über Fahrhabe oder Totschlag geregelt, und zwar in England, so dass 3, 4 nicht [wie ich gegen meine Übersetzung mit früheren Erklärern in II 639 Sp. 2 n. 8c annahm] in 4 sich fortsetzt. Denn eine Rubrik steht in Ld, Q (also in lq?) vor 4. Auch lässt sich 5, 1ff. nicht mit 3, 4 verbinden, sondern nimmt offenbar England als Tatort an

Of a Norse ship; against Nicolas Hist. Engl. navy I 21. —From here on the procedure in a dispute between one member of each of the two contracting parties over movables or homicide is regulated, and that in England, so that 3, 4 does not continue in 4 [as I assumed, contrary to my translation, with earlier commentators in II 639 col. 2 n. 8c]. For a rubric stands before 4 in Ld and Q (and so in lq?). Nor can 5, 1ff. be connected with 3, 4; rather it evidently assumes England as the scene of the deed
Vielleicht ist neben blosser Gewalt auch nach friedlich begonnenem Handel Zwist über die Zahlung gemeint: Kauffahrer und Pirat war damals oft identisch
Perhaps, besides mere violence, a dispute over payment after trading begun peacefully is also meant: merchant and pirate were often one and the same at that time
Die Tatsache des Beraubtseins durch irgendwelche Dänen macht nicht etwa das Heer dem Englischen Kläger solidarisch haftbar
The fact of having been robbed by some Danes or other does not, say, make the army jointly liable to the English plaintiff

‘auf’ stand in lq (da in Q, on Ld Rb, während of B und daraus Ld Text); also vielleicht ist of (‘durch’, s. Toller of IV) nur B's Verschlechterung; während lq den Handel des Engländers auf Nordischem Schiffe meinte, dachte B an Plünderung durch ein solches

‘on’ stood in lq (since in Q, on Ld Rb, whereas of B and, from it, Ld text); so perhaps of (‘by’, see Toller of IV) is merely B’s corruption; whereas lq meant the Englishman’s trading on board a Norse ship, B was thinking of plundering by one
Kapitän und Schiffsherr; vgl. Gl Schiff 3a. 8c. Er verantwortet gerichtlich, was auf seinem Fahrzeug geschieht; s. d. Seewurf
Captain and ship-owner; cf. Gl Schiff 3a. 8c. He is legally answerable for what happens on his vessel; see Seewurf
Vgl. Gl Eideshelfer 32. 36.—Über dieses nur bekräftigende gangan s. d. Wb 9
Cf. Gl Eideshelfer 32. 36.—On this merely corroborative gangan see that word in Wb 9

Q meint laut erit, das Eine Kaufgeschäft zwischen den zweien an Bord. Mir erscheint jetzt wie in I 223 diese Auffassung richtig. Frühere, und im Glossar (o. ¹) auch ich, verstanden ‘wie es soeben [in 3, 3] abgemacht wurde’, verlegten also den Handel in jenes neutrale Land

Q, as erit shows, means the single business transaction between the two on board. This interpretation now seems to me correct, as in I 223. Earlier scholars, and I too in the Glossary (above ¹), understood ‘as was just agreed [in 3, 3]’, and thus placed the trading in that neutral country
The difference in the readings is noteworthy. Ld’s rubric reads on, Q in.
Lit. ‘steersman.’ It seems to have been the usual practice for the commander to steer the ship, even in the case of kings, cf. Egilssaga, Ch. 56.
In this construction the chief person is sometimes included in the number and sometimes not—an ambiguity which it is not easy to account for, see BT. p. 933, s.v. sum, I b, α and β.

Liebermann (iii. p. 153), in view of the Latin translation prelocutum erit, understands the clause to refer to a transaction between an Englishman and a Northman regarding which a dispute has afterwards arisen. It seems more natural, however, to connect it with 3, 3, above.
